title: WriteBatch construction with explicit column-family handles is about 3.8% slower after 15873b1f
body:
I followed up on commit `15873b1f` in my machine, comparing the unmodified commit with its immediate parent. In measurements collected on September 12, 2026, construction of WriteBatch objects across 20 column families took **3.799% longer [95% CI: 3.519%, 4.079%]**, with after slower in all 16 confirmation pairs. This is a constructed batch-construction workload, not an exact reproduction of the original BackupEngine loop or a claim about complete `DB::Write` performance.

## Environment and measurement

The machine has two Intel Xeon Gold 6430 CPUs, 64 physical cores and 128 logical CPUs, and runs Ubuntu 22.04, Linux `5.15.130-0515130-generic`, glibc 2.35 and GCC 11.4. Data directories were on NVMe. The measured thread was pinned to logical CPU 17; the orchestration process used CPU 13. The governor was `performance`, Turbo was enabled, and frequency was not locked. This was a shared host, not an isolated machine; a running `rshim` service consumed approximately one CPU and was not stopped or repinned.

Both sides used unmodified static libraries built with the same Make options:

```bash
make -C "$SOURCE" -j32 static_lib DEBUG_LEVEL=0 PORTABLE=1 \
  DISABLE_WARNING_AS_ERROR=1 CC=gcc-11 CXX=g++-11
```

The library's release optimization level was `-O2`; the test programs used `-O3 -DNDEBUG -fno-rtti -std=c++17` and linked against their respective revision's headers and static library. The tested snapshots identify themselves as 10.1.0. These are tested source revisions, not a claim that every release with those version numbers is affected.

After screening, the selected workload received 16 new confirmation pairs. Within each pair, the versions ran serially in alternating before/after and after/before order, each with a fresh database. Screening samples were not pooled with confirmation samples. Means below are arithmetic means; percentage changes are geometric means of paired after/before ratios, with two-sided 95% Student t intervals calculated on the log ratios. These intervals describe within-host repeatability, not variation across machines. All confirmation pairs are included in the attached CSV files.

## Workload and results

- Before: `da8eba8b4927ae92be24b4dab3417187ca979d66`
- After: `15873b1fdd3a4aa7a21825616623e4fb482443e7` (New CF option disallow_memtable_writes, #13431)
- Component: `WriteBatch::Put` with an explicit `ColumnFamilyHandle`.

The workload creates the default column family and 19 ordinary column families, then precomputes 2,000,000 keys in `key_exit:%09d` format, numbered from 0 to 1,999,999. Each value contains 16 `v` bytes. No column family has `disallow_memtable_writes` enabled; this test uses the normal memtable, not VectorRep.

The timed loop constructs and retains WriteBatch objects, adding 256 records per batch with `Put(handles[j % 20], keys[j], value)`. There are 7,813 batches; the last contains 128 records. The holding vector is reserved before timing. Timing includes batch allocation, record insertion and retaining the batches, but excludes key generation, database/column-family creation, `DB::Write`, destruction and verification.

| Metric | Before mean | After mean | Paired change | 95% confidence interval |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Construction elapsed time | 0.125328 s | 0.130089 s | +3.799% | [+3.519%, +4.079%] |
| Process CPU time | 0.125300 s | 0.130074 s | +3.810% | [+3.535%, +4.086%] |

After was slower in **16/16 confirmation pairs**, with every pair exceeding 3%. The corresponding construction-throughput change is **-3.660%**. This does **not** mean complete database writes are 3.8% slower. In separate confirmation workloads using VectorRep, complete batched writes slowed by 1.496% with 20 column families and 0.624% with 256 column families. The original repeated BackupEngine open/create-backup/destroy workload did not show a stable regression in the previous rerun.

After timing, the program applies every retained batch to the database, checks a sequence-number increase of exactly 2,000,000, verifies every key and value, flushes all column families, closes/reopens the database and verifies everything again. The post-timing writes disable WAL and are flushed to SST before reopening; this is a correctness check, not a measurement of durable-write latency.

The commit adds a `disallow_memtable_writes` check in `WriteBatchInternal::GetColumnFamilyIdAndTimestampSize()`. Each explicit-handle Put in this workload reaches that path even though the option remains false. The additional MemTableInserter check is outside this test's timed region. This narrows the observation to batch construction containing the new column-family check, but I have not performed an ablation that attributes the entire difference to that check. It also measures a different scope from the full-write `db_bench` test in the commit description.

The exact tested program is attached as `upstream-attachments-20260913/rocks_focus.cc`. After building it as described below, a single trial is:

```bash
taskset -c 17 "$BINARY" "$RUN" batch-only 2000000 256 20 1 1 off 0 1
```

`$RUN` must be a new trial directory. The program creates its dataset itself; no external database snapshot is required. The printed `seconds` field, not the duration of the whole process, is the measured construction time.

## Building the attached test program

Use separate clean source trees for the before and after commits listed above. Set `$SOURCE` to the relevant checkout, `$HARNESS` to the attached `.cc` file and `$BINARY` to a distinct output executable. The test program for this workload is `rocks_focus.cc`. The tested link command was:

```bash
g++-11 -std=c++17 -O3 -DNDEBUG -fno-rtti -I"$SOURCE/include" \
  "$HARNESS" "$SOURCE/librocksdb.a" \
  -pthread -ldl -lrt -lsnappy -lz -lbz2 -lzstd -o "$BINARY"
```

Use matching development libraries on both sides; build metadata in the attachment records the detected features. Run versions serially and counterbalance their order, rather than comparing one before run with one after run. These commands reproduce the workload; recompilation on another machine is not expected to reproduce the archived executable hashes or identical percentages.

## Attachments

[rocksdb-15873b1f-attachments-20260913.tar.gz](rocksdb-15873b1f-attachments-20260913.tar.gz) 

[rocksdb-15873b1f-attachments-20260913.tar.gz](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/32158701/rocksdb-15873b1f-attachments-20260913.tar.gz)

contains this commit's standalone reports and supporting material:

- The exact tested `rocks_focus.cc`, copied without modification.
- Native result JSON, program output, command and property records for all 32 construction-confirmation runs, plus the 16-pair CSV.
- Construction-confirmation statistics, original summary objects for the same commit's full-write controls, independently recalculated construction statistics, the relevant commit diff, build provenance and environment information.
- A commit-specific provenance record, checksum manifest and evidence verification record.

The `historical-scripts` directory preserves original orchestration scripts as provenance; their historical paths are not prerequisites for running the C++ workload described here. This standalone bundle does not require another report or attachment, and excludes database directories and binaries. No sampled flamegraphs were collected for this case.

title: Add configurable largest-memtable flush policies to WriteBufferManager (#15047)
body:
Summary:
A shared WriteBufferManager currently triggers flushing in the DB whose write notices memory
pressure and selects the oldest mutable memtable. With many column families or DBs sharing the
manager, this can repeatedly flush small memtables while a much larger memory consumer remains
 untouched, resulting in unnecessary flushes and slower memory reclamation.

 This change adds configurable WriteBufferFlushPolicy modes:

  - kFlushOldest: preserves the existing behavior and remains the default.
  - kFlushLargest: flushes the largest eligible mutable memtable in the current DB.
  - kFlushLargestAcrossDBs: compares reclaimable memory across all DBs sharing the WBM and
    schedules a flush on the largest consumer.

 For cross-DB selection, DBs register lightweight flush initiators with the shared WBM. The
 selected DB performs the memtable switch asynchronously on the low-priority pool, using a non-
 blocking write-thread join to avoid waiting behind a write stall. If a writer reaches the hard
 stall threshold after deferring to another DB, it also seals a local memtable to guarantee
 forward progress.

title: Validate HyperClock key sizes before hashing
body:
## Summary

Why this change is required:

HyperClockCache supports exactly 16-byte cache keys. Its fixed-width hash unconditionally reads 16 bytes from the supplied Slice, so key size must be validated before hashing. Because Cache methods accept runtime keys, this is a public input contract rather than a private control-flow invariant.

Previous behavior:

The generic ShardedCache implementation computed the hash before dispatching to ClockCacheShard. ComputeHash had a debug assertion for the 16-byte requirement, while shard methods performed the release checks only after hashing. Under NDEBUG, a short key could therefore cause a 16-byte out-of-bounds read before the shard returned its documented failure result. Oversized keys were also hashed before being rejected.

New behavior:

HyperClock validates key size before hashing for Insert, Lookup, CreateStandalone, and Erase. Invalid keys retain the established API results: Status::NotSupported for Insert, nullptr for Lookup and CreateStandalone, and no operation for Erase. Valid 16-byte keys are unchanged.

Implementation:

Override the four key-based operations in BaseHyperClockCache and perform one UNLIKELY size check before calling ShardedCache. Replace the later shard-level release checks with assertions, while retaining the ComputeHash assertion. These assertions now protect internal post-validation invariants without duplicating the release check on the valid hot path.

Safety boundaries and unsupported cases:

The change covers every public HyperClock operation that hashes a caller-provided key. Handle-based operations do not accept keys and are unaffected. HyperClock still does not support variable-length keys, and the change does not alter its key format, hash function, or behavior for valid keys. Internal callers that bypass the public boundary must continue to satisfy the 16-byte invariant and are checked in debug builds.

Performance:

A/B cache_bench runs compared release builds of this source tree and parent d699ffbd5 with fixed seeds, pinned CPUs, and alternating parent/candidate order. Median candidate throughput versus parent was +0.61% for one-thread Auto HyperClock lookup, +0.27% for one-thread Fixed HyperClock lookup, and +0.27% for a one-thread Auto HyperClock mixed workload.

The eight-thread Auto HyperClock mixed workload was noisier. Short and longer experiments measured aggregate median changes of -1.25% and -1.17%; paired medians were -0.65% and -0.74%, with roughly 2-3% run-to-run variation. These results do not establish a material regression, but they do not rule out a sub-1% high-concurrency slowdown. A focused perf stat sample retired approximately four fewer instructions per lookup in the candidate, and disassembly confirmed the validation override was inlined without an extra function call.

Tests performed and known limitations:
    
Ran both Auto and Fixed ClockCacheTest.Misc cases and all CacheTest.InvalidKeySize variants. Repeated the combined focused tests with ASSERT_STATUS_CHECKED=1 and ran make check-sources. The full make check C++ suite completed without test failures; its two auxiliary environment/baseline checks were rerun successfully with Ruby on PATH and API_COMPAT_REF pinned to parent d699ffbd5.
    
The public regression covers short and oversized keys across all four operations and verifies that invalid operations leave an existing valid entry intact. The performance measurements were collected on one shared host rather than a dedicated benchmark machine. cache_bench exercised Lookup, Insert, and Erase but not CreateStandalone; CreateStandalone is covered by the unit test. The concurrent sub-1% signal would require more controlled benchmarking to resolve.


## Test plan

- ClockCacheTest.Misc for Auto and Fixed HyperClock
- CacheTest.InvalidKeySize variants
- ASSERT_STATUS_CHECKED=1 combined focused run
- make check-sources
- Full make check, with auxiliary workflow-YAML and C-API checks rerun using their required local context
- DEBUG_LEVEL=0 production compilation
- Alternating A/B cache_bench runs for Auto and Fixed HyperClock, including single-thread lookup and single- and eight-thread mixed workloads
- perf stat instruction and cycle sampling on the focused and mixed workloads

title: Recover from poisoned WAL handles on remote file systems (#15193)
body:
Summary:

Keep `DB::Write`'s existing immediate `IOError` contract while allowing RocksDB to recover safely when a remote file system reports that a WAL handle is permanently unusable.

### Behavior changes

#### 1. Recovering from a poisoned remote WAL handle

- **Why required:** A remote file system can permanently poison a WAL handle after an I/O failure. Retrying that handle cannot succeed and leaves the database write-stopped.
- **Previous behavior:** RocksDB retried the same WAL handle during recovery.
- **New behavior:** The remote file system marks the failure as file-scoped. RocksDB creates a replacement WAL, atomically persists all state that could depend on the failed WAL, and then removes the quarantined WAL handles from active use. Physical file deletion remains part of normal cleanup.

#### 2. Preserving an indeterminate WAL write outcome

- **Why required:** A WAL record can reach storage before the append returns `IOError`; the application therefore cannot know whether that write took effect.
- **Previous behavior:** Recovery could reuse the failed write group's sequence numbers, allowing a later acknowledged write to overlap a record that might already be in the WAL. The public write API did not state this indeterminate outcome.
- **New behavior:** `DB::Write` still returns the original `IOError` immediately and does not retry the logical batch. Recovery carries the highest ambiguous sequence forward and durably reserves it before admitting later writes. The public API now documents that an `IOError` may mean the write succeeded or failed and that non-idempotent writes must not be retried blindly.

#### 3. Keeping all column families on one recovery boundary

- **Why required:** A write batch can update multiple column families. Retiring its WAL after independently persisting only some column families can expose a partially applied batch after reopen.
- **Previous behavior:** With `atomic_flush=false`, recovery could persist column families independently before abandoning the WAL.
- **New behavior:** File-scoped WAL recovery force-flushes every live column family atomically and verifies that each one advanced beyond the failed WAL before writers are retired or writes resume.

#### 4. Merging concurrent WAL failures

- **Why required:** Another WAL write can fail while an earlier recovery attempt temporarily releases the DB mutex.
- **Previous behavior:** A later failed WAL cutoff or ambiguous sequence could be overwritten or cleared by the earlier recovery attempt.
- **New behavior:** Each error episode monotonically merges the largest failed WAL cutoff and ambiguous sequence. Recovery clears the quarantine cutoff only if no concurrent failure extended it; otherwise the newer failure remains write-stopping for the next attempt.

#### 5. Retaining file scope through `NoSpace` recovery

- **Why required:** `NoSpace` can still identify one permanently unusable WAL handle.
- **Previous behavior:** The `SstFileManager` recovery path entered generic recovery without carrying the failed WAL context.
- **New behavior:** File-scoped `NoSpace` carries the same cutoff and sequence evidence through the `SstFileManager` path as other file-scoped WAL errors.

#### 6. Scoping recovery context to one error episode

- **Why required:** A completed recovery must not affect a later unrelated background error.
- **Previous behavior:** WAL recovery context could remain latched after `ClearBGError` succeeded.
- **New behavior:** Successful background-error clearing resets the context. A failed recovery retains it so a later retry has the same safety information.

#### 7. Preserving successful `SyncWAL` metadata

- **Why required:** A healthy WAL can finish syncing while a separate recovery error already exists.
- **Previous behavior:** `SyncWAL` could return the existing background error before applying the successful WAL's `VersionEdit`, dropping its MANIFEST update.
- **New behavior:** `SyncWAL` skips quarantined writers, applies metadata for successfully synced healthy WALs, and only then returns any existing recovery error.

#### 8. Classifying only the intended remote-file-system failure

- **Why required:** File-scoped recovery is valid only for an actual WAL `IOError` from a handle whose ownership is still valid.
- **Previous behavior:** Poison state could be queried before ownership fencing was resolved, and file scope could be stamped onto a non-I/O status.
- **New behavior:** Ownership fencing is resolved first, poison state is queried afterward, and only an actual `IOError` can be classified as file-scoped. `IOFenced` remains fatal.

#### 9. Preserving `paranoid_checks=false` retry behavior

- **Why required:** Non-paranoid mode historically cleared a writer's sticky error so a later operation could retry after storage recovered.
- **Previous behavior:** Avoiding reclassification of a cached synthetic writer error also bypassed `WALIOStatusCheck`, so later `SyncWAL` calls kept returning the stale error.
- **New behavior:** A cached error still fails the current `SyncWAL` call, but the non-paranoid path resets the writer for a later retry without setting a background error or entering file-scoped recovery.

#### 10. Preserving async WAL precreation across recovery

- **Why required:** A precreated WAL is an unpublished replacement and is not the active WAL. Recovery can also consume the prepared slot while background work is stopped.
- **Previous behavior:** A file-scoped failure while creating or starting the unpublished replacement was attributed to the active WAL, unnecessarily quarantining it. After successful recovery consumed a prepared WAL, the next slot was not replenished, so the following rotation created its WAL synchronously.
- **New behavior:** Only an active WAL `WriteBuffer()` failure attaches the active-WAL cutoff. A failed unpublished candidate is discarded while the current WAL remains active, and successful recovery schedules the next async precreation after `ClearBGError()` re-enables background work.

### Implementation

- Carry `DBRecoverContext` through generic, `NoSpace`, and `SstFileManager` recovery, merging WAL cutoffs and failed write-group sequences independently of error severity.
- Publish a lock-free quarantine cutoff used by write and sync paths; replace even an empty failed current WAL; persist ambiguous sequence reservations; force and verify an atomic all-column-family flush; and detach quarantined writers only after that durable boundary.
- Keep successful healthy-WAL tracking edits in `SyncWAL`, reset completed recovery context, and preserve legacy non-paranoid writer reset behavior.
- Distinguish failures on an unpublished replacement WAL from failures flushing the active WAL. Log the failed replacement identity, keep the active WAL out of quarantine, and replenish the async-precreation slot after successful recovery.
- Classify poisoned remote-file-system handles after ownership fencing and only for `IOError`.
- Add lifecycle logging and a state-machine comment covering quarantine, sequence reservation, replacement, atomic persistence, retirement, and concurrent-error handoff.
- Add an opt-in `db_stress` mode that injects file-scoped faults only into WAL writes, disables WAL tracking in that mode, validates unsupported direct invocations, and sanitizes crash-test parameters to the supported recovery envelope. A small fraction of ordinary non-specialized crash-test runs select this mode automatically; existing stress behavior is unchanged when the flag is off.
- Make the concurrent-error regression test hold the initial background flush until `SyncWAL` records the intended older-WAL error, preventing scheduler-dependent retirement of the test WAL before fault injection.

### Safety boundaries and unsupported cases

- Automatic file-scoped WAL recovery fails closed with `NotSupported` for manual WAL flush, 2PC/transactions, two write queues, pipelined or unordered writes, WAL recycling, WAL TTL or size retention, either WAL-tracking mode, or blob direct writes.
- Unsupported recovery leaves the DB write-stopped. `DB::Resume()` returns `NotSupported`; after correcting the I/O condition, operational recovery requires close and reopen.
- The failed logical batch is never retried. Generic indeterminate WAL errors may reserve sequence numbers without invoking file-scoped retirement.
- Failed recovery attempts retain their context. Only a successful `ClearBGError` resets it.
- Physical WAL deletion is not part of the correctness boundary; normal obsolete-file cleanup removes files later.
- Async WAL precreation remains disabled with WAL recycling. A prepared WAL is unpublished until its start records succeed; failure before installation does not make the active WAL file-scoped.
- The new stress mode is test-only and defaults off, so normal `db_stress` and database operation without an error are unchanged.
- Automatic stress-profile selection is limited to fully parsed, supported configurations. Explicit targeted runs reject options files and other unsupported combinations.

### Tests and known limitations

- `arc f --take-formatters --enforce-lint-clean` passes.
- All 67 `error_handler_fs_test` cases pass under `ASSERT_STATUS_CHECKED=1`, including the two new async-precreation recovery tests.
- All 5 existing `AsyncWalPrecreate*` tests pass.
- The two new async-precreation recovery tests completed 65 consecutive forced-context-switch iterations before the required 60-second cap interrupted iteration 66; no completed iteration failed.
- All 8 `fault_injection_fs_test` cases pass, including the new scope/isolation test; all 42 `db_crashtest_test.py` cases pass.
- The previously flaky concurrent-sequence test passes in the exact seven-way CI shard and in 40 consecutive repetitions under concurrent load after synchronizing the initial flush.
- The non-paranoid cached-error regression passed 100 consecutive `COERCE_CONTEXT_SWITCH` iterations earlier on this diff. All 13 remote file system adapter tests also passed earlier on this diff.
- Two bounded in-process multi-column-family stress runs passed verification. The non-atomic run completed 7 quarantine/replacement/retirement/resume cycles; the atomic-flush run completed 15 cycles, including 14 persisted ambiguous-sequence reservations.
- A 20-second black-box crash/reopen dry run exited successfully and decoded 7 injected WAL faults in one interval. A later run completed 8 recovery cycles before its final verification reached the 60-second cap.
- The full crash/stress matrix and TSAN were not run. `make check-sources` and the sparse checkout's `fbcode//rocks:format_check` are unavailable because they assume a Git checkout or the target is absent; `arc f` and `clang-format-diff` were clean.

title: Add DB::ApplyLsmEdit(), a declarative LSM edit primitive
body:
Summary:
`IngestExternalFile()` is a policy engine that *derives* a `VersionEdit` from
files: you hand it paths, it probes the LSM level by level and decides where
each file lands and what sequence number it gets. That works well when the
caller has no opinion about shape, and badly when it does. Two things fall out
of it that keep costing us real I/O:

- **Placement is emergent, not stated.** A caller that already has a valid LSM
  -- because it built one in a scratch instance -- cannot transplant it. It has
  to flatten that LSM into a single non-overlapping sorted run first, purely so
  the placement heuristic will accept it. That flattening is a full rewrite of
  data that was already correct.
- **Ranges must be file-aligned.** `atomic_replace_range` refuses a range that
  any existing file only partly overlaps, even when that file holds no key
  inside the range. The fix available today is to compact the range so a file
  boundary lands on it -- again, rewriting correct data to move a boundary.

This diff adds the primitive that expresses the operation directly instead:

    Status DB::ApplyLsmEdit(const LsmEditOptions&, const std::vector<LsmEdit>&);

An `LsmEdit` names a column family, a half-open key range, and the files that
will occupy it, each carrying the level it goes to. RocksDB validates that
arrangement rather than deriving one, and commits every edit in the call as a
single atomic MANIFEST write. Files keep the sequence numbers they were written
with; no global seqno is assigned.

Two capabilities are new, and they are what the callers above are missing:

**Declared placement.** `LsmEditFile::level` is an input. A multi-level set of
files installs with its layering intact, level 0 included -- overlapping level 0
runs are ordered by their position in `add_files`, oldest first. RocksDB checks
that the level has room (no surviving file's key range overlaps there) and
rejects the edit otherwise.

**Straddler probing.** Installing files with their own sequence numbers is only
sound if nothing already live sits in the range, so the edit removes every file
contained in it and *probes* every file that merely crosses its boundary. The
probe is one seek per straddling file, plus a range-tombstone check, and it
either proves the file holds nothing in the range -- in which case the file is
retained untouched -- or fails the edit. Where the alternative was compacting
live data to move a file boundary, this is a handful of block reads.

Implementation reuses `ExternalSstFileIngestionJob` rather than adding a
parallel path: the job gains an optional `LsmEditJobSpec` carrying the declared
levels, `AssignLevelAndSeqnoForIngestedFile()` validates the declared level
instead of searching when one is present, and the existing
`atomic_replace_range` machinery supplies range containment, memtable overlap,
pending-compaction conflict detection and the delete side of the edit.

The API is EXPERIMENTAL and has no C or Java binding yet, matching
`PrepareFileIngestion()`.

title: Add stress scan witness diagnostics
body:
Summary:
## Why
PrefixScan and MultiScan verification failures are difficult to reconstruct from the terminal assertion alone. The iterator options, bounds, seeks, preparation state, and immediately preceding movements are often the evidence needed to distinguish a database defect from an invalid test assumption.

## Why the existing recovery trace is not enough
The expected-state trace exists to reconstruct the expected database state after recovery. It preserves ordered write batches and deliberately filters out reads and iterator seeks, then recovery consumes a sequence-number-selected prefix. Consequently it contains none of the scan-specific evidence needed here: read options, bounds, seek targets, iterator validity, lazy-value preparation, movements, or the exact mismatch state. Scan witnesses capture that bounded human-readable context only when a verification failure needs it; they are best effort, are never replayed, and do not alter the recovery trace or its failure semantics.

## Previous behavior
The scan paths emitted generic failure output but did not retain a focused bounded witness of iterator setup and state transitions. Adding instrumentation naively would also format diagnostic strings on the normal path even when disabled and could create one file per failing operation.

## New behavior
An opt-in bounded ScanWitnessLog records scan configuration and recent iterator events for PrefixScan and MultiScan variants. On a qualifying failure it writes the latest complete witness for that DB, PID, thread, and scan type. The operation ordinal remains in the file contents. Repeated failures atomically replace the fixed witness rather than creating unbounded files.

## Implementation
The witness captures sanitized read options, input ranges, bounds, seeks, movement, PrepareValue results, iterator status, keys, value size and hash, and wide-column state. MultiScan tracks whether the current primary iterator value was actually prepared so failure snapshots report accurate state. Disabled witnesses avoid scan-label ownership, range formatting, expected-count formatting in release builds, and numeric iterator-label conversion. Witness writes share the per-thread diagnostic I/O-disable latch with breadcrumbs, write to a fixed temporary path, close, and rename over the final file. Entry counts are capped at 65,536. A formatting-only follow-up normalized all touched C++ lines with the repository clang-format rules.

## Safety and unsupported cases
The feature is stress-tool-only and raw db_stress keeps it disabled by default. It observes public iterator state and does not change database contents, expected-state tracing, recovery replay, iterator decisions, or fault-injection outcomes. Diagnostic I/O remains best effort and cannot fail the workload. Files are bounded per retained PID, thread, and scan type. The witness covers the instrumented PrefixScan and MultiScan implementations only and is not a general RocksDB trace. Files are not fsynced and therefore are not a power-loss durability mechanism.

## Tests and limitations
Validated with 47 tools/db_crashtest_test.py tests, exact-candidate debug and release db_stress builds, arc lint over the complete stack, oversized-entry rejection, and clean independent correctness reviews of the final integrated stack. make check-sources is unavailable because it invokes Git in this Sapling checkout; equivalent added-line hygiene checks pass. Only the newest complete witness per DB, PID, thread, and scan type is retained, so later failures intentionally replace earlier witnesses.

title: Add db_stress operation breadcrumbs (#15194)
body:
Summary:

## Why
Intermittent db_stress and db_crashtest failures often report only the terminal assertion, after the operations that established the failing state have scrolled out of logs. Recovery validation traces serve a different replay contract and do not provide this bounded, human-readable per-thread history.

## Why the existing recovery trace is not enough
The existing expected-state trace is a correctness oracle for recovery: after an expected-state checkpoint it records ordered write batches, and recovery replays the prefix implied by the database sequence number. Reads and iterator seeks are deliberately filtered out, trace-write failures are fatal, and the trace is machine-consumed rather than intended as a concise failure narrative. It therefore cannot show which read, scan, maintenance operation, or operation phase immediately preceded an assertion. Breadcrumbs fill that observability gap with a bounded, human-readable, per-thread snapshot. They are best effort, never replayed, and remain independent of the recovery-validation contract.

## Previous behavior
db_stress did not retain a bounded per-thread operation history. db_crashtest did not automatically provision a local directory for these artifacts. Repeated diagnostic writes could accumulate across failed runs, and the expected-state trace remained the only persistence mechanism associated with recovery validation.

## New behavior
An opt-in per-thread breadcrumb ring records recent operation begin, context, and end events. db_crashtest enables breadcrumbs by default, assigns a local diagnostics directory, retains the newest eight process groups after failed child runs, and removes managed artifacts after success. Periodic snapshots keep the existing configured cadence. Each worker preserves its first verification-failure snapshot; the final driver fallback flushes only threads that did not already attempt that snapshot.

## Implementation
Breadcrumb snapshots write a complete ring to a fixed temporary file, close it, and rename it over the prior final snapshot. One helper now owns ring insertion and wrap bookkeeping. A single per-thread failure-flush method is used by both `RecordOperationEnd()` and the driver fallback, making the first failure snapshot idempotent while preserving fallback coverage for failures outside a scoped operation. `RecordOperationEnd()` uses one atomic failure-state snapshot for both the record marker and the flush decision. The `uint64` periodic-flush interval accepts its full declared range; zero remains the value that disables periodic flushing. Enabled operation-context formatting writes directly into the reused ring-slot string and uses `std::to_chars` for integers; disabled call sites retain their early guard and avoid formatting or container construction. The vector and initializer-list entry points share one implementation. Diagnostics-directory validation and creation are isolated in a helper to keep setup control flow shallow without changing its one-time behavior. Any diagnostic filesystem failure disables later breadcrumb and scan-witness I/O attempts for that thread without affecting the workload result. Entry counts are capped at 65,536. Auto-directory pruning and cleanup accept only exact generated filename schemas, reject symlink roots, preserve unrelated files and explicit user directories, and never retain more than eight PID groups. A formatting-only follow-up normalized all touched C++ lines with the repository clang-format rules.

## Safety and unsupported cases
This is stress-tool-only diagnostic behavior. Raw db_stress keeps breadcrumbs disabled by default. Diagnostic setup, writes, rename, pruning, and cleanup are best effort and never determine database or verification outcomes. Periodic full-ring file I/O remains enabled at the requested interval. These files are not recovery-validation traces, are not replayed, and provide no durability guarantee across power loss because they are not fsynced. Explicit diagnostics directories are never automatically pruned or removed. Nested operation scopes are not supported; current instrumented execution paths do not nest them.

## Tests and limitations
Validated with 47 tools/db_crashtest_test.py tests, exact-candidate debug and release db_stress builds, arc lint over the complete stack, oversized-entry rejection at 65,537, acceptance of periodic interval 4,294,967,296, an atomic breadcrumb snapshot smoke test, paired release benchmarks, and independent correctness reviews with no findings on each final candidate. In five CPU-pinned alternating pairs, enabled breadcrumbs improved from a 3.14 s baseline median to 1.95 s (-37.9%); disabled medians were 1.31 s and 1.32 s (+0.8%, within noise). make check-sources is unavailable in this Sapling checkout because it invokes Git internally; equivalent added-line hygiene checks passed. The artifact is a bounded latest snapshot rather than a complete operation log.

title: Revamp sst_dump recompress for serious benchmarking
body:
Summary:
Extends `sst_dump --command=recompress` from a basic evaluation tool to a serious compression benchmarking tool, also able to evaluate interactions with table format options affecting uncompressed sizes and compressibility.

For each input file it now emits a benchmark "baseline" entry for the file as stored, followed by one entry per compression type / strategy / level, reporting compressed and uncompressed data-block sizes, index sizes, compression ratio, and both wall-clock and CPU time for the write and read tests. All data/index sizes are block payload excluding block trailers, so compressed vs uncompressed figures are on a consistent basis. The input's uncompressed data size is inferred from decompression statistics, so it is available even for files that don't persist it. That inference is exact when the input's index blocks are stored uncompressed (the default); with enable_index_compression it can be slightly overstated because index-block decompression is also counted (see the CAVEAT in GetInputBenchmarkMeasurement).

New capabilities:
* `--json` for machine-readable output. It is self-contained: each measurement carries the compression manager id and the full CompressionOptions, and every baseline/measurement entry is tagged with its input file path so multiple input files produce one valid document.
* `--compression_strategy=` to sweep a list of CompressionOptions strategy values (multiplied with levels), useful for side-channel configuration of custom compressors.
* `--show_properties` additionally dumps the input and last recompressed output TableProperties.

To keep measurements meaningful, a quiet throw-away priming build runs whenever the compression type changes (warming up the compressor), CPU time is measured process-wide so parallel compression worker threads (compression_parallel_threads > 1) are included rather than undercounted, and the timed windows are kept tight: the write build is fed from an in-memory copy of the input so its timing excludes reading and decompressing the input (and is independent of block-cache state), and the read timing covers only the block reads. The timings for compression and decompression do include BlockBasedTable overheads but this is considered reasonable--if not preferable--to the intended application of finding the overall most efficient settings related to compression.

Also fixes a latent bug exposed by measuring several compression types in one run: the recompressed table was read back through the shared block cache under a common (unknown) cache-key identity, so a later type could get a cache hit on a stale block from an earlier, differently-compressed table and fail with "Corruption: bad entry in block". The read-back now bypasses the block cache.

Also fixes a typo in CLAUDE.md.

Intended follow-up: persist TableProperties::uncompressed_data_size. It is already computed in memory at build time but is never written to the properties block (PropertyBlockBuilder::AddTableProperty has no entry for it), so it reads back as 0 for on-disk files. Persisting it (backward compatible; old files read 0) would fix `data uncompressed size: 0` for all property readers and let this tool read the value directly, removing the decompression-ticker inference above and its index-compression caveat for all but pre-existing files.

Test Plan:
Added sst_dump_test cases exercising recompress with --show_properties and with --json.

Ad hoc manual testing against real SST files: verified the text benchmark table, and piped `--json` output through `json_pp` to confirm well-formed JSON, for a single file, a directory of multiple SST files, and combined with --show_properties, --output_hex, --compression_strategy, and --block_based_table_options. Confirmed process CPU time exceeds wall-clock write time with --compression_parallel_threads=4 (and matches at =1).

title: Document that WriteOptions::sync flushes the WAL buffer with manual_wal_flush
body:
With `DBOptions::manual_wal_flush=true`, a `Write()` with `WriteOptions::sync=true` does flush the WAL buffer to the file and sync it before returning, so the data is durable, even though `log::Writer::AddRecord` skips its automatic `Flush()` in this mode. The reason is that the write path syncs the WAL file with `WritableFileWriter::Sync()`, which flushes all buffered WAL data to the file before fsyncing: in `DBImpl::WriteGroupToWAL` without `two_write_queues`, and via `FlushWAL(true)` / `SyncWAL()` with `two_write_queues`.

Nothing in the documentation promised this, so this adds the guarantee to the comments on `DBOptions::manual_wal_flush` and `WriteOptions::sync`, and points out that `DB::SyncWAL()` alone does not flush the buffer.

Doc-only change. Fixes #12287

title: Fix docs for SetBackgroundThreads vs max_background_jobs
body:
The comment on `Env::SetBackgroundThreads` did not explain how the thread pool sizes relate to `max_background_jobs`, and the comment on `max_background_jobs` did not document how the job limit is split between flushes and compactions, leaving users to find the split in `DBImpl::GetBGJobLimits`. In particular, the common pattern of calling `SetBackgroundThreads` with the same value for the HIGH and LOW pools and setting `max_background_jobs` to that value only leaves idle threads, since `max_background_jobs` only caps concurrent jobs and DB open already grows the pools to accommodate its split.

This documents the relationship in both comments, including the split: with only `max_background_jobs` set, the limit is `max(1, max_background_jobs / 4)` concurrent flushes and `max(1, max_background_jobs - flushes)` concurrent compactions.

Doc-only change. Fixes #11097

title: Add DB::DisableWalDeletions()/EnableWalDeletions() for WAL-scoped retention
body:
## Summary

Adds `DB::DisableWalDeletions()` / `DB::EnableWalDeletions()`, a WAL-scoped
counterpart to the existing `DisableFileDeletions()` / `EnableFileDeletions()`
pair. While the gate is engaged, obsolete WALs are **not deleted, not archived,
not purged from the archive directory, and not recycled**. Writes, flushes,
compactions, and reclamation of every other file type continue normally.

The gate is a counter, so independent callers can hold it concurrently, exactly
like `DisableFileDeletions()`.

## Motivation

The WAL lifecycle is already designed with replication in mind — the wiki notes
that an archived WAL "is not immediately deleted ... to allow transaction log
iterator to keep reading the WAL and send it to the follower for replay". But
the knobs that actually implement that delay are a poor fit for an external
consumer that knows precisely when it is done reading:

* `DBOptions::WAL_ttl_seconds` / `WAL_size_limit_MB` are **static** options, so
  they cannot be opened and closed at runtime around a specific operation. They
  are also **time/space-driven guesses** — a consumer cannot express "I am still
  reading this, do not remove it yet".
* Both only apply to the **archival path**. With the default `0 / 0`, an
  obsolete WAL is deleted in place and never reaches `archive/` at all, so there
  is no retention window to speak of.
* The only runtime mechanism today is `DisableFileDeletions()`, which is
  all-file-types: `FindObsoleteFiles()` returns immediately, so obsolete SSTs,
  blob files and MANIFESTs pile up alongside the WALs. That means space
  amplification, stale `GetLiveFiles()`/checkpoint sets and slower recovery — a
  heavy price for "let me read a few WALs undisturbed".

This leaves a gap for WAL-tailing consumers: streaming replication, CDC, the
WAL phase of an incremental backup, or shipping WALs to cold storage. This PR
fills it with a gate that is WAL-scoped, runtime-switchable, and counted.

## Design

**New state.** `DBImpl::disable_wal_deletions_`, an `int` under `mutex_`,
deliberately **orthogonal** to `disable_delete_obsolete_files_` — neither counter
is nested inside or derived from the other. The relationship is a logical AND:
WALs are reclaimed only when *both* are zero. `EnableWalDeletions()` gets that
for free because it routes through `FindObsoleteFiles()`, which already returns
early while the all-files gate is held.

**Snapshot, not live read.** The gate is propagated to the purge via
`JobContext::wal_deletions_disabled`, captured under the mutex in
`FindObsoleteFiles()` rather than read from the member inside
`PurgeObsoleteFiles()`. Collection happens under `mutex_` but the purge runs
without it, so a snapshot keeps a single purge round internally consistent: a
round collected *before* the gate was engaged is allowed to finish, and no round
can observe the gate flip halfway through and end up half-applied. This follows
the existing pattern used for `log_number`, `prev_log_number` and
`manifest_file_number`.

**Gate points.** Three explicit, one implicit:

1. The `kWalFile` `keep` condition in `PurgeObsoleteFiles()` — covers both
   `log_delete_files` and full-scan candidates.
2. The trailing `wal_manager_.PurgeObsoleteWALFiles()` call — covers TTL/size
   cleanup of the `archive/` directory.
3. `SwitchMemtable()`'s recycling condition. This one is the least obvious and
   the most important: recycling is *not* deletion, it is
   `ReuseWritableFile(new_log, old_log)`, which **renames** the retained WAL onto
   a fresh log number. Without gating it, a path the caller was told would be
   retained silently disappears from under them.
4. `ArchiveWALFile()` is covered **implicitly** — it is only reachable on the
   `keep == false` branch, so while the gate is held an obsolete WAL stays where
   it is in `wal_dir` instead of being moved into `archive/`.

**Why `EnableWalDeletions()` forces a full scan.** While the gate is held,
`FindObsoleteFiles()` still pops obsolete WALs off `alive_wal_files_`, dequeues
them from `logs_`, closes their writers and subtracts from `wals_total_size_`.
Only the *physical* removal is suppressed. So the retained files have left
in-memory accounting, and the counter-zero path calls
`FindObsoleteFiles(&job_context, /*force=*/true)` to rediscover them from the
filesystem. Closing the writers also means the retained WALs are complete and
readable, and since `WalManager::GetSortedWalFiles()` scans the filesystem rather
than `alive_wal_files_`, they remain enumerable through `GetSortedWalFiles()` —
which is the point of the feature.

## Semantics and known trade-offs

Stating these explicitly, since a couple are deliberate choices rather than
oversights:

* **`max_total_wal_size` will not throttle on retained bytes.** Because
  `wals_total_size_` keeps draining while the files stay on disk, the
  `SwitchWAL()` write-stall trigger does not fire for them. Holding the gate for
  a long time can therefore grow WAL disk usage without bound; bounding the
  retention window is the caller's responsibility. This currently lives in a code
  comment — happy to surface it in the `db.h` doc block if reviewers prefer
  (I left it out to keep the public comment tight).
* **The counter is not persisted.** If a caller disables and then closes without
  re-enabling, the counter is simply zero after restart. This is self-healing
  rather than leaky: `Recover()` already runs `FindObsoleteFiles(force=true)` +
  `PurgeObsoleteFiles()` on a successful non-read-only open, so WALs left behind
  by an unbalanced disable are reclaimed on the next open.
* **Interaction with `error_if_wal_file_exists` / `error_if_data_exists_in_wals`.**
  Both checks iterate every on-disk WAL and fail on any non-empty file, so a
  retained obsolete WAL will make
  `rocksdb_open_for_read_only(..., error_if_wal_file_exists=1)` fail. This is
  identical to the pre-existing behaviour of `DisableFileDeletions()` and is not
  introduced here (`DBImplReadOnly` itself returns `NotSupported` for the new
  API).
* **In-flight purges are not cancelled**, matching the documented behaviour of
  `DisableFileDeletions()`.

### Recovery safety

Retained WALs do end up in the recovery input set, so this was checked end to
end:

* `Recover()` enumerates **every** `kWalFile` in `wal_dir` with no
  `min_log_number` filter, so retained obsolete WALs are passed to
  `RecoverLogFiles()`.
* But `SetupLogFilesRecovery()` computes
  `min_wal_number = MinLogNumberToKeep()` (max'd with
  `MinLogNumberWithUnflushedData()` in non-2PC mode) and `ProcessLogFile()` skips
  `wal_number < min_wal_number`, so stale WALs are never replayed.
* `WalSet::CheckWals()` only verifies that MANIFEST-tracked WALs are present;
  extra on-disk logs are explicitly tolerated (documented in `wal_edit.h` and
  covered by `WalSetTest.CheckWals`).
* Archived WALs live in `wal_dir/archive/` and the recovery scan uses
  `do_not_recurse = true`, so they never enter recovery.

## Compatibility

* The two new `DB` virtuals are **non-pure with a `NotSupported` default**. This
  matches an established pattern in `db.h` — `Close()`, `Resume()`,
  `ResetStats()`, `FlushWAL()`, `LockWAL()`, `UnlockWAL()`,
  `VerifyFileChecksums()`, `TryCatchUpWithPrimary()` and others are declared the
  same way. `LockWAL()`/`UnlockWAL()` are the closest analogue: a paired
  WAL-scoped runtime switch whose doc uses the same "each call that returns OK
  must eventually be followed by a corresponding call" contract. Out-of-tree `DB`
  subclasses therefore keep compiling unchanged.
* `StackableDB` forwards both, which covers `TransactionDB`,
  `OptimisticTransactionDB`, `DBWithTTL` and `BlobDB`/`BlobDBImpl`. `BlobDBImpl`
  needs no dedicated override: its explicit `Disable/EnableFileDeletions`
  overrides exist only to add blob-GC gating, which is unrelated to WALs.
* `DBImplReadOnly`, `DBImplSecondary` (and thus `DBImplFollower`) and
  `CompactedDBImpl` return `NotSupported`.
* **C API** goes through the spec-driven generator: only
  `tools/c_api_gen/spec.json` and the checked-in generated fragments are edited
  by hand; `include/rocksdb/c.h` and `db/c.cc` are `@generated` output.
* Release note added at
  `unreleased_history/public_api_changes/wal_deletions.md`.

## Testing

New C++ tests in `db/obsolete_files_test.cc`:

* `WalDeletionsPreserveLogsButDeleteSsts` — the core contract, run over
  `{separate wal_dir, same wal_dir} × {avoid_unnecessary_blocking_io on, off}`:
  a compacted-away SST is reclaimed while the WAL is retained; releasing the
  WAL gate does **not** bypass the all-files gate, and vice versa; extra
  `EnableWalDeletions()` calls do not underflow the counter and a subsequent
  disable still works.
* `WalDeletionsWrappersAndReopen` — `StackableDB` forwarding, retention across a
  close/reopen cycle, and `NotSupported` from a read-only instance.
* `WalDeletionsPreventRecycling` — with `recycle_log_file_num = 2`, proves the
  retained WAL is neither recycled nor deleted while the gate is held, and that
  recycling resumes afterwards. Since recycling renames rather than deletes, a
  missing file alone cannot distinguish the two outcomes, so the test observes
  the `DBImpl::CreateWAL:BeforeReuseWritableFile1` sync point to prove the pooled
  WAL is genuinely consumed by recycling once the gate is released.
* `WalDeletionsProtectArchivedLogs` — over `{WAL_ttl_seconds, WAL_size_limit_MB}`,
  verifies already-archived WALs are protected, no new archival happens while
  disabled, and both TTL- and size-driven purge resume afterwards (uses mock
  sleep to satisfy `WalManager`'s purge-interval rate limiter).

title: Doc bug: CustomFilterPolicy example
Learn RocksDB traffic patterns for offpeak telemetry (#15175)
body:
Summary:

Collect DB-wide foreground read/write ticker deltas through the stats-history sampling path and build a persisted 15-minute UTC traffic profile using an exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA).

`dynamic_offpeak_percentile` is the single feature switch: `0` disables dynamic off-peak telemetry, while values from `1` through `50` enable it and select the quietest percentile. Enabling requires statistics and `stats_persist_period_sec` in the range `[1, 900]`; the same validation applies both at DB open and through `SetDBOptions()`.

How samples fill the model

`DynamicOffpeakModel::AddSample()` converts each interval into byte and operation rates, splits it at UTC day boundaries, and passes each same-day piece to `AddSegment()`. `AddSegment()` divides the piece among overlapping 15-minute buckets according to covered seconds.

```
Sample 00:10-00:25: 9,000 bytes / 900 sec = 10 B/s

00:00         00:15         00:30
|-- bucket 0 --|-- bucket 1 --|
          |---------|
        00:10     00:25

bucket 0 gets 5 min  * 10 B/s = 3,000 B
bucket 1 gets 10 min * 10 B/s = 6,000 B
```

Operations are apportioned the same way. When sampling enters the next UTC day, a day with at least 90% coverage updates each bucket using `25% completed day + 75% previous EWMA`.

How the window is selected

```
96 bucket EWMAs
       |
       v
trailing 4-bucket / 60-minute smoothing
       |
       v
rank bytes and operations separately
       |
       v
average the ranks: 0 = quiet, 1 = busy
       |
       v
mark the configured quietest percentile eligible
       |
       v
select the longest circular eligible run
```

The circular search allows a window to cross midnight:

```
UTC:       23:15  23:30  23:45  00:00  00:15
eligible:    no     yes    yes    yes     no
                     |------ selected ------|

learned window: 23:30-00:14
```

Threshold ties may make slightly more than the configured percentile eligible. Equal-length runs prefer the lower average score and then the earlier UTC start.

What is persisted

The learned model is stored as a versioned binary blob in the MANIFEST:

```
DynamicOffpeakModel
|
+-- metadata
|   +-- encoding version
|   +-- trained day count
|   +-- last-day coverage percent
|   +-- last update timestamp
|   +-- learned UTC window
|
+-- 96 learned 15-minute buckets
    +-- known flag
    +-- byte-rate EWMA
    +-- operation-rate EWMA
```

This is roughly 1.6 KiB and contains the compact learned profile rather than raw samples. Partial data for the current day and the latest observation are intentionally not persisted, so they restart empty after DB reopen. Disabling collection retains the persisted learned profile so it remains available if the option is enabled again.

Expose the advisory learned window, predicted byte/operation rates, and latest observed rates through `rocksdb.dynamic-offpeak` for manual validation and future ODS export. This does not modify `daily_offpeak_time_utc`, periodic compaction scoring, or any other compaction policy.

title: rocksdbjni fat JAR omits license and notice materials for bundled native code
body:
## Summary

The `org.rocksdb:rocksdbjni` fat JAR appears to omit the license texts and attribution notices applicable to RocksDB, LevelDB-derived code, and statically linked native dependencies.

I verified this against:

- `rocksdbjni:9.8.4` (version brought transitively to my project by the Spark version I am using)
- `rocksdbjni:10.10.1`, which Maven Central metadata currently identifies as the latest/release version; and
- the JNI build and packaging definitions in the latest upstream RocksDB release, `v11.8.1`.

The published `10.10.1` JAR contains native binaries for multiple platforms but no `LICENSE`, `NOTICE`, `COPYING`, `DEPENDENCIES`, or third-party notice material.

The current `v11.8.1` source still uses the same packaging approach, so the problem appears to remain present in the latest upstream build definition.

## No separate Maven Central license bundle

The [Maven Central directory for `10.10.1`](https://repo.maven.apache.org/maven2/org/rocksdb/rocksdbjni/10.10.1/) does not seem to provide a separate `LICENSE`, `NOTICE`, `COPYING`, third-party notices file, or legal-material classifier or bundle.

The sources classifier also contains no license- or notice-named entry.

The [POM](https://repo.maven.apache.org/maven2/org/rocksdb/rocksdbjni/10.10.1/rocksdbjni-10.10.1.pom) declares RocksDB's Apache License 2.0 and GPLv2 options using URLs. However, it does not include:

- The actual license texts
- `LICENSE.leveldb`
- Copyright notices and disclaimers for LevelDB-derived code
- License and attribution information for statically linked native dependencies

## Current build evidence

Both the `v10.10.1` and [`v11.8.1`](https://github.com/facebook/rocksdb/blob/v11.8.1/Makefile) Makefiles build the JNI native library with these static compression libraries:

```makefile
JAVA_COMPRESSIONS = libz.a libbz2.a libsnappy.a liblz4.a libzstd.a
```

In `v11.8.1`, the configured versions are:

| Library | Version |
|---|---:|
| zlib | 1.3.1 |
| bzip2 | 1.0.8 |
| Snappy | 1.2.2 |
| LZ4 | 1.10.0 |
| Zstd | 1.5.7 |

The release-JAR targets add history files, native libraries, and Java classes, but do not add any of the project or dependency license files.

## Why this matters

`rocksdbjni` redistributes compiled native implementations for several platforms, including statically linked third-party code.

RocksDB's Apache-2.0 option and several applicable BSD-style licenses contain redistribution conditions involving the provision or reproduction of license, copyright, conditions, and disclaimer material.

Because neither the binary JAR nor a companion Maven artifact supplies that material, downstream projects cannot simply preserve and redistribute the upstream legal files. Each downstream distributor must independently reconstruct the applicable license and notice set. This makes compliant binary redistribution unnecessarily difficult and creates a risk that applications embedding the fat JAR will omit required materials.

## Expected result

The published binary JARs should contain an authoritative legal-material set, for example:

```text
META-INF/LICENSE
META-INF/NOTICE
META-INF/licenses/LICENSE.rocksdb-apache-2.0
META-INF/licenses/LICENSE.leveldb
META-INF/licenses/LICENSE.zlib
META-INF/licenses/LICENSE.bzip2
META-INF/licenses/LICENSE.snappy
META-INF/licenses/LICENSE.lz4
```

title: Skip duration reporting for no-op POSIX file flushes
body:
## Description

`ReportDuration()` in `TestFileOperationListener` (`db/listener_test.cc`) asserts that every file operation has a strictly positive duration:

```cpp
ASSERT_GT(info.duration.count(), 0);
```

`PosixWritableFile::Flush()` is an intentional no-op — it performs no underlying operation and returns `IOStatus::OK()` immediately. Since there may be effectively no work between the start and finish timestamps, the measured duration can legitimately be `0ns`. On Apple Silicon, this happens consistently, causing `EventListenerTest.OnFileOperationTest` to fail:

```text
Expected: (info.duration.count()) > (0), actual: 0 vs 0
```

This PR removes the `ReportDuration(info)` call from `OnFileFlushFinish` only. Duration reporting remains unchanged for the other file-operation callbacks.

Relaxing the assertion globally to `ASSERT_GE(..., 0)` was considered, but that would weaken the check for operations where a positive duration is still expected. Scoping the change specifically to the known no-op `Flush()` keeps the existing duration checks meaningful for the other operations.

## Motivation and Context

Addresses #15139.

`EventListenerTest` uses the default POSIX environment path through `DBTestBase`, so the failure occurs on the actual POSIX file implementation rather than being caused by test-specific file-operation behavior.

This is related to the behavior discussed in #7133, where the POSIX no-op `Flush()` was also identified as a case where a zero duration can occur.

## Testing

Verified on an Apple Silicon M2 Mac:

```text
❯ ./listener_test --gtest_filter=EventListenerTest.OnFileOperationTest

[----------] Global test environment set-up.
```

title: Fix self-deadlock with unordered_write + manual_wal_flush (#15097)
body:
## Summary

Fixes #15097.

Any WAL-enabled write on a DB opened with `unordered_write=true`,
`manual_wal_flush=true`, and `two_write_queues=false` (the default)
deadlocks. `WriteImplWALOnly` is used whenever `unordered_write_` is set,
regardless of `two_write_queues_`, and it always routes through
`ConcurrentWriteGroupToWAL`, which unconditionally locks
`wal_write_mutex_` before calling `WriteToWAL`. `WriteToWAL`, however,
inferred whether the caller already held the mutex from
`two_write_queues_` alone (`needs_locking = manual_wal_flush_ &&
!two_write_queues_`), so with `two_write_queues_ == false` it tried to
lock the same (non-recursive) mutex again on the same thread, hanging
forever in `pthread_mutex_lock`.

- Replaced the flawed `two_write_queues_` inference with an explicit
  `wal_write_mutex_held` parameter on `WriteToWAL`, set correctly at each
  of its three call sites: `WriteGroupToWAL` (mutex not held), the
  recovery dummy-write in `DBImpl::Open` (mutex not held), and
  `ConcurrentWriteGroupToWAL` (mutex always held, since it locks
  unconditionally right before calling `WriteToWAL`).
- While in the same function, fixed an adjacent lock leak: an early
  return on a `MaybeAddUserDefinedTimestampSizeRecord()` failure skipped
  `wal_write_mutex_.Unlock()` when `needs_locking` was true, which would
  leave the mutex permanently locked on that (narrower) I/O-error path
  too.
- No behavior change for the pre-existing `two_write_queues_` callers:
  `ConcurrentWriteGroupToWAL` already always holds the mutex before
  calling `WriteToWAL` regardless of `two_write_queues_`, and
  `WriteGroupToWAL` is only ever reached when `two_write_queues_` is
  false, so `needs_locking` evaluates identically to before in both
  cases.

## Test plan

- Added `DBWriteTestUnparameterized.UnorderedWriteManualWalFlushDoesNotDeadlock`,
  which puts a key on a DB configured with
  `unordered_write=true, manual_wal_flush=true` and waits with a 30s
  bound (rather than joining directly) since the point of the test is to
  detect a hang. Confirmed it fails after the 30s bound on the
  pre-fix code and passes in ~30ms with the fix.
- Full `db_write_test` suite: 53/53 pass.
- Full `db_wal_test` suite: 1982/1982 pass.
- `make check-sources` clean; changed files formatted with `clang-format`.

title: Fix native ReadOptions leak in RocksDB.close() (Java)
body:
## Summary
`RocksDB.close()` disposes owned column family handles and its own native handle, but never releases `defaultReadOptions_`,  the `ReadOptions` object eagerly created in the field declaration and used internally by `newIterator()`. This leaks one native `ReadOptions` object per opened `RocksDB` instance for the lifetime of the JVM, since there is no finalizer or `Cleaner` fallback anywhere in the `RocksObject` hierarchy, an explicit `close()` call is the only path to native cleanup, and this one was never wired up.

## Fix
Added `defaultReadOptions_.close()` inside `close()`'s existing cleanup block, alongside `disposeInternal()`.

## Testing
Added `closeReleasesDefaultReadOptions` to `RocksDBTest.java`, asserting `defaultReadOptions_.isOwningHandle()` transitions from `true` to `false` across a `close()` call. Full Java suite passes (1241 tests, 0 failures).

Fixes #15036

title: Re-acquire db_mutex_ in MemPurge early return path
body:
While tracing FlushJob::MemPurge I noticed the early return for a flush-time compaction filter that doesn't ignore snapshots comes back without re-locking db_mutex_. MemPurge unlocks the mutex at the top and every other path re-locks before returning, because Run falls back to WriteLevel0Table() on a failed mempurge and that function asserts the lock. So on this path the fallback ran unlocked - an AssertHeld failure in debug builds, and in release an unlock of a mutex the thread doesn't hold, which can clobber another thread's critical section.

The fix locks again before returning, and drops the filter first so its user-defined destructor doesn't execute under the DB mutex. Fixes #14198.

I could not run the C++ test suite on this machine (Windows, no toolchain for rocksdb), so this was verified by reading the lock/unlock flow in flush_job.cc.

title: Cast to unsigned char before isspace() in a few trim/tokenize paths
body:
Fixes #7809.

A handful of whitespace-trimming and tokenizing loops pass a plain `char` straight into `isspace()`, and that's only defined behavior when the value is representable as `unsigned char` or equals `EOF`. On platforms where `char` is signed (the usual case), a UTF-8 continuation byte turns into a negative `int` and the result is unspecified from that point on.

The original reporter hit this as an MSVC debug-CRT assertion when opening a DB whose name ends in a non-ASCII character. `TrimAndRemoveComment` runs `isspace()` over the temporary options file content, which embeds the DB name, and a trailing multi-byte UTF-8 character trips the assertion. A comment on the issue pointed out the same pattern also exists in `util::trim()` and `OptionTypeInfo::NextToken`, so I fixed all three.

Each call site now goes through `lossless_cast<unsigned char>`, following `cast_util.h`'s own guidance to prefer it over a bare `static_cast` for this kind of conversion. Extended the existing `StringUtilTest.Trim` case with a string ending in a two-byte UTF-8 character.

One honest caveat: I don't have a Windows machine handy, so I couldn't reproduce the actual MSVC assertion locally, only confirm the fix compiles and the existing/new tests pass. That said, the change addresses genuine undefined behavior either way, independent of whether any particular libc's ctype table happens to tolerate an out-of-range argument without visibly misbehaving, which is exactly why this bug showed up as version- and platform-dependent to begin with.

Ran `string_util_test` and `options_test` locally, both green. `make check-sources` and `clang-format` also clean.

title: Fix MSVC C4702 warnings in trie index factory
body:
## Summary

Remove the two `return nullptr` statements that follow unconditional `abort()` calls in the deprecated `TrieIndexFactory` overloads.

## Why

These overloads are intentionally non-returning, as documented by their existing comments. MSVC diagnoses each trailing return as unreachable code (C4702), which breaks Windows builds when warnings are treated as errors. Since `abort()` is non-returning, deleting the unreachable statements preserves the intended behavior and keeps warning-as-error coverage intact.

This was found while packaging RocksDB 11.8.1 for conda-forge. I searched the current RocksDB issues and pull requests for C4702, unreachable-code, and trie-index fixes and found no existing report or patch; current `main` still contains both returns.

## Validation

- the complete conda-forge RocksDB 11.8.1 matrix passed with this patch, including the native [Windows build](https://github.com/conda-forge/rocksdb-feedstock/actions/runs/31420671001/job/93560346459)

body:
Summary:
When a database is opened read-only and qualifies for compacted DB mode (such as a single SST file or all files in a single level without merge operators), read operations are handled by CompactedDBImpl.

In CompactedDBImpl::Get and CompactedDBImpl::MultiGet, GetContext was being constructed with

title: Cross-key coalescing for lazy wide-column blob reads
body:
Summary:
Follow-up (Phase 3) to the experimental lazy wide-column read API (DB::GetEntityLazy / DB::MultiGetEntityLazy). A MultiGetEntityLazy batch now resolves blob references across keys with coalesced I/O instead of key-by-key.

- MultiGetEntityLazy acquires one SuperVersion and one consistent (implicit) sequence number for the whole batch via MultiCFSnapshot (as multi-CF iterators do) and transfers a single shared per-column-family pin into the LazyWideColumnsBatch, replacing the former per-key SuperVersion + explicit-snapshot loop. Single column family for now; a cross-CF ColumnFamily** overload remains a follow-up (the batch already models a per-CF pin map).
- LazyWideColumnsBatch::MultiResolve groups the batch's reads by (Version, blob file) for separate-file references and by SST for embedded references, and issues one coalesced read per group -- for whole-column and byte-range reads alike -- caching whole values in each entity's resolver and pinning partial reads directly.
- Adds the coalesced blob-read primitives this needs (none existed before): range-aware BlobFileReader::MultiGetBlobRange / BlobSource::MultiGetBlobRange / Version::MultiGetBlobLazy for separate-file references, and an embedded (SimpleGen2) batch read path (blob_gen2_format batch readers + BlobSource::MultiGetSimpleGen2Blob[Range] + BlockBasedTable::MultiGetSameFileBlob). Whole-value separate-file coalescing reuses the existing MultiGetBlob. The batch readers sort their requests by file offset before issuing the underlying MultiRead (which requires ascending offsets), and gen2 checksum verification is factored into one helper shared by the scalar and batch readers.
- The hot non-lazy Get / MultiGet / iterator / compaction paths are untouched: the new multis are lazy-only, and the GetImpl change is gated on a new opt-in GetImplOptions field (an injected shared SuperVersion + sequence number) used only by the batched lazy read.
- Blob read failures on these paths (short reads, invalid offsets, out-of-range requests, compression mismatches) now carry file/offset/size and expected-vs-actual context, mirroring the block-checksum diagnostics.
- db_bench gains a multireadrandomentitylazy benchmark for measuring the coalesced batch path.

No public API change, so this is a performance follow-up to the still-recent lazy API rather than a new feature.

Test Plan:
New unit tests in db/wide/db_lazy_entity_test.cc assert cross-key coalescing via a blob-file / SST MultiRead counter added to the test FileSystem wrapper:
- N whole-column separate-file reads across keys in one blob file collapse to a single coalesced MultiRead (and the fetched values are cached, so a repeat read does no further blob I/O);
- N byte-range separate-file reads collapse to one MultiRead, save the un-read bytes (rocksdb.blobdb.lazy.partial.bytes.saved), and never fill the blob cache;
- embedded (same-file) reads across keys in one SST collapse to one MultiRead over that SST;
- an out-of-order embedded batch (reads issued in descending record offset) still resolves correctly in one coalesced read, covering the batch readers' internal offset sort;
- a mixed batch (inline + whole + byte-range across keys) returns the correct bytes for each read;
- a batched MultiGetEntityLazy + one MultiResolve matches resolving each key via a separate GetEntityLazy. The existing db_stress lazy-vs-eager differential (MaybeTestMultiGetEntityLazy) exercises the new batched read and cross-key MultiResolve unchanged (same public API).

title: Add Compressor::MaybeOverrideCompressionOptions() omnibus hook
body:
Summary:
Compressor::GetRecommendedParallelThreads() was a narrow hook for the one CompressionOptions field (parallel_threads) that the SST builder, rather than the Compressor, is responsible for applying. Other such options exist (max_compressed_bytes_per_kb, auto_skip, auto_skip_min_sample_every), and more may be added. This replaces the narrow hook with an omnibus MaybeOverrideCompressionOptions(CompressionOptions*) that a Compressor can override to steer any of them. GetRecommendedParallelThreads() is now deprecated; the default implementation of the new method still honors an overridden GetRecommendedParallelThreads(), so existing custom Compressors keep working. CompressorWrapper forwards the new method; built-in compressors are unchanged (picked up via the default bridge).

The block-based table builder now consults the data-block compressor (falling back to the base compressor before the data-block compressor exists, e.g. during dictionary sampling, where parallel compression does not start anyway) and applies the possibly-overridden options. While here, the builder records the effective (post-override) options in the rocksdb.compression_options table property instead of the pre-override configured options, and the two affected Rep members (compression_parallel_threads, max_compressed_bytes_per_kb) are set exactly once from the effective options -- with poisoned defaults so any use before they are computed surfaces -- rather than initialized in the member list and overwritten later.

Test Plan:
Added DBCompressionTest.CompressorOverridesCompressionOptions, which installs a Compressor that overrides MaybeOverrideCompressionOptions() to force parallel_threads and verifies via the builder's sync point that parallel compression starts with the overridden thread count, then reads the data back. The existing GetRecommendedParallelThreads and
ConfiguredCompressionTypeRecordedInProperties tests continue to cover the deprecated bridge and the table-property recording respectively.

title: Add opt-in graceful WAL rotation for GetUpdatesSince iterator
body:
## Summary
Adds an opt-in, immutable DBOption `wal_iterator_tail_rotations` (default false). When enabled, the `WalIterator` returned by `GetUpdatesSince` continues a run wherever it can correctly do so, instead of ending the run as soon as its snapshot of WAL files is out of date. A consumer that keeps up with the write rate can then stay on one iterator across WAL rotations, instead of rebuilding one — and paying an `O(#WAL files)` directory rescan on every rotation.

 When the iterator exhausts its file snapshot while LastSequence() has advanced, it:
  1. Asks for the next WAL after its last file via a NextWalForTailFn callback; the current implementation (DBImpl::FindNextLiveWalForTail) reads the immediate successor from alive_wal_files_ under mutex_ — no directory I/O.
  2. Opens it via WalManager::PrepareWalForTail and reads its first sequence number directly from disk.
  3. Continues the run only if that first sequence is exactly current_last_seq_ + 1.
  4. Otherwise ends the run with Status::TryAgain as before, and the caller rebuilds via GetUpdatesSince(seq) — which also searches the archive, so
  it can succeed where the live-only fast path declined.

The option is transitional: it exists to stage the rollout, the default is expected to flip to true, and the option is expected to be removed (marked DEPRECATED at introduction). It is defined by the promise rather than the mechanism, so later extensions (e.g. consulting the archive) land under the same flag.

## Motivation
On every WAL rotation the iterator hits EOF, returns `TryAgain`, and the poller must call `GetUpdatesSince` again — which runs `GetSortedWalFiles` (O(N) `GetChildren` + `GetFileSize` over live + archive dirs). With ~143 archived WALs at ~178 MB each and rotations every ~15-20s, this causes regular 300-400ms latency spikes that block followers.

## Key design decisions

- **Opt-in via immutable DBOption** (`wal_iterator_fast_rotation`), set in the OPTIONS file. Default off.
- **Advances to the immediate successor**, not the newest WAL — so multiple live rotations are walked one at a time (no data skipped).
- **Sequence continuity check** (`first_seq == current_last_seq_ + 1`) is the correctness guard — any gap causes `TryAgain` fallback.
- **Trims consumed `WalFile` entries** exclusively in the fast-rotation path so long-lived iterators don't leak memory. The existing snapshot-advance path is untouched.
- **Callback plumbing** — the iterator receives a `NextLiveWalFn` callback (bound in `DBImpl::GetUpdatesSince` when the option is on) that reads `alive_wal_files_` under `mutex_` and calls `WalManager::PrepareNextWalForTail`. Zero cost when the option is off (null callback, never invoked).

## Files changed
- `include/rocksdb/options.h` — new `wal_iterator_fast_rotation` bool in `DBOptions`
- `options/db_options.{h,cc}` — `ImmutableDBOptions` member, type info map, ctor, Dump()
- `options/options_helper.cc` — reverse copy in `BuildDBOptions()`
- `options/options_settable_test.cc` — settable test strings
- `db/transaction_log_impl.{h,cc}` — `NextLiveWalFn` type alias, callback member, ctor param, `NextImpl` fast-rotation branch + trim
- `db/wal_manager.{h,cc}` — `PrepareNextWalForTail` helper, `GetUpdatesSince` callback param
- `db/db_impl/db_impl.cc` — callback lambda binding when option is on
- `db/db_log_iter_test.cc` — 6 new tests
- `unreleased_history/public_api_changes/wal_iterator_fast_rotation.md`

## Test plan

- [x] 6 unit tests covering: single rotation continues, multiple live rotations continue, purged successor falls back, opt-in off preserves behavior, empty new WAL falls back, sequence gap falls back
- [x] `--gtest_repeat=5` passes (no flakiness)
- [x] `options_settable_test` passes (option round-trips through OPTIONS file)

title: Handle async prefetch failures safely
body:
## Summary

FilePrefetchBuffer owns the I/O handles, callback state, and scratch buffers used by asynchronous prefetch reads. Poll and AbortIO are runtime operations whose successful return establishes callback completion; an error does not.

Problem: cancellation results were guarded only by assertions. Release builds could ignore an AbortIO failure and clear or destroy request state that an outstanding callback still referenced. Poll failure likewise destroyed the handle even though completion was not guaranteed. Separately, callback completion status was ignored, including synchronous inline completion, and failure to submit a later buffer could leave earlier requests from the same multi-buffer prefetch active.

Impact: callbacks could access released FilePrefetchBuffer state, resulting in use-after-free, crashes, or memory corruption. Async read errors could be masked and failed or partial buffer state treated as usable. A failed multi-buffer operation could also leave sibling I/O running after the caller had received an error.

Fix: make cancellation and outdated-data helpers return Status and propagate poll, abort, and submission failures without releasing live handles, buffers, or callback state. Poll errors preserve the request for a later poll or abort. The destructor attempts AbortIO, falls back to Poll, and terminates with diagnostics if neither can establish safe completion.

Record callback status only when completion fails, consume it after Poll confirms callback completion, clear failed buffers, and handle default inline ReadAsync completion immediately. When a later multi-buffer submission fails, remove the failed buffer and abort earlier sibling requests. Expected cancellation status is discarded safely, while successful requests retain the allocation-free path. Synchronous fallback, EOF behavior, and public APIs remain unchanged.

Tests: add a controlled async filesystem covering AbortAllIOs and outdated-I/O failure propagation, Poll failure lifetime preservation, destructor fallback, inline and background completion errors, and later-submission cleanup. The complete prefetch_test suite passes normally and with ASSERT_STATUS_CHECKED=1; source and whitespace checks pass as well.


## Test plan

- Complete `prefetch_test` suite.
- Complete `prefetch_test` suite with `ASSERT_STATUS_CHECKED=1`.
